completedPhaseClaims.summary: Reliability, flakiness, resource and operational-soundness pass over the delivered namespace-lock harness. Verdict UNSTABLE, qualified: no active instability was measured (all four TestNamespaceLock_ guards PASS, nslock package 0.214s, integration-light lane exit 0), and the label is not PARTIALLY_STABLE only because the two substantive findings require authoring a test, which is bubbles.test's artifact rather than stabilize's. ST-1 (MEDIUM): the release path has no guard, and no test written against the current callers could give it one, because every caller registers t.Cleanup(pool.Close) before Acquire registers the unlock, so closing the pool releases the lock whether or not pg_advisory_unlock worked -- a working unlock and a broken one produce the same observable. The package doc names a leaked lock (a HUNG suite) as the worst design outcome, and that is the one property nothing tests. ST-2 (MEDIUM): the LIFO backstop that bounds a failed unlock to one test is a caller convention, not a package property, and callsite_contract_test.go enforces the Acquire call but not the pool-close ordering; ST-1 and ST-2 compound under a TestMain-scoped pool, which is the ordinary optimisation that relaxing -p 1 would motivate. ST-3 (LOW-MEDIUM): acquireTimeout 60s is not budgeted against go test -timeout 300s; the largest acquiring package has 4 acquire points (240s worst case), so a fifth reaches the package timeout and replaces the helper's addressed t.Fatalf with a goroutine-dump panic exactly when contention becomes real. ST-4 (LOW, latent): a second Acquire on one *testing.T pins a different pooled connection, so it self-deadlocks for 60s; unreachable today but resetKnowledgeStatsTables acquires from inside a helper taking t, which is the shape that eventually gets called twice. ST-5/ST-6 informational: ABBA deadlock is impossible with one locked namespace and the 60s bound would convert any future one into a bounded named failure; there is no runtime cliff under -p 1, and the cliff is conditional on relaxing it. ST-7: a hypothesised defect was REFUTED by measurement rather than shipped.

completedPhaseClaims.summary: Security and compliance pass over the delivered namespace-lock harness. Across the nine files this packet changed, NO security defect was found, and that clean result is stated plainly rather than padded with a manufactured finding. Five surfaces were verified rather than assumed. (1) SQL construction: the namespace string never reaches SQL at all -- Key() converts it to an int64 before any statement is built, and all three statements bind that int64 as $1, so the injection class is eliminated by type rather than by escaping; two scans over all nine files (SQL built by concatenation/Sprintf, and the namespace reaching any Exec/QueryRow/Query) both returned no match. (2) FNV collision: acceptable here because of the DIRECTION of the failure -- a collision in an exclusive-lock keyspace causes two unrelated things to serialise and can never cause contenders that need one lock to believe they hold different ones, so it degrades liveness, never safety; there is additionally no untrusted input path into Key(), every namespace argument being a compile-time constant. (3) Credentials: nslock.go never reads DATABASE_URL; the openPool this packet added never passes dbURL to a format verb, and the non-obvious path -- pgconn's ParseConfigError, which does carry the ConnString -- redacts the password in Error() via redactPW, verified in pgx v5.9.2 module source at pgconn/errors.go:127 and 216-228. (4) Production reachability: the helper is unreachable in the shipped artifact by two independent mechanisms, either sufficient alone -- nothing outside tests/ imports it, so it is absent from the import graph of smackerel-core and alertmanager-ntfy-bridge; and the root Dockerfile is multi-stage, with COPY . . landing in the builder while the runtime stage copies only compiled binaries. (5) Denial of service: a leaked advisory lock cannot wedge PostgreSQL beyond the test lane, bounded by acquireTimeout 60s, the lane's -timeout 300s, pool.Close() at test end, and PostgreSQL's release of session locks on connection teardown.

completedPhaseClaims.unprovenClaimNote: RESOLVED 2026-08-22 by bubbles.validate; the original text is preserved in the sentence that follows. This phase recorded, correctly, that it had NOT computed the FNV-1a hash and would not assert one from memory, so whether Key("smackerel_self") collides with production's migration lock pg_advisory_lock(42) in internal/db/migrate.go stayed open -- a real question, because advisory locks share one global keyspace per database. bubbles.validate has now MEASURED it. Key() is Go's fnv.New64a() reinterpreted as a signed integer, read from source at tests/integration/nslock/nslock.go:105-109 rather than assumed. Because a reimplementation of FNV can agree with itself and still be wrong about what the repository actually computes, the computation was first ANCHORED to a value measured live from PostgreSQL: the recorded pg_advisory_unlock(-3753811720078285197) for namespace nslock-guard-namespace, which it reproduces EXACTLY. RESULT: Key("smackerel_self") = 7135712157784582883 (unsigned == int64), production's constant is 42 confirmed at internal/db/migrate.go:27, and they DO NOT COLLIDE. The key is also positive, so ST-7's negative-key concern does not arise for this namespace at all. This closes the question WITHOUT changing S2's conclusion: S2 argued that a collision degrades liveness and never safety whichever way the number fell, so the measurement removes a hypothetical rather than repairing a weak link. Evidence: report.md, section 'Certification Evidence'.

executionHistory.note: Reliability and operational-soundness diagnosis of the delivered namespace-lock harness. Nothing was mutated: no test authored, no source file changed, no probe created, so no restore was needed and no `trap ... EXIT` was used anywhere. Measured this phase: all four TestNamespaceLock_ guards PASS with the nslock package at 0.214s and the whole integration-light lane at exit 0; the lane passes `-p 1 -tags integration -v -count=1 -timeout 300s` while the helper's acquireTimeout is 60s, and the two constants live in different files with neither referencing the other; acquire points per package are nslock 4, openknowledge 3, e2e/openknowledge 2, integration 1, selfknowledge 1; every caller registers t.Cleanup(pool.Close) inside its pool helper before Acquire, so LIFO does put the unlock first as the package doc claims; the lane hardcodes -count=1 and exposes only --go-run, so no zero-mutation in-process release probe was available and none was manufactured. Seven findings, all ROUTED rather than fixed, because each needs a test or lane-script change owned by another agent. The load-bearing one is ST-1: release is the single property no guard asserts, and it is not merely untested but structurally unobservable through the current callers, since pool.Close would release the lock whether or not pg_advisory_unlock worked -- so a broken unlock and a working one produce the same result. ST-2 shows the LIFO backstop is a caller convention that callsite_contract_test.go does not enforce, and the two compound under a TestMain-scoped pool. ST-3 quantifies the unbudgeted 60s-vs-300s timeout relationship at one acquire of headroom.
